question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(4)
$$

So, we have

- one $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =4,$ and

- one $1\times 1$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =4.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(4) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(4) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =4.$ 

Now, computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $z$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

$$
(A-4I)z=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=y,
$$

and, therefore,

$$
(A-4I)^{2}z=(A-4I)y=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.
